records.name: PRAXIS-VirtualCell
records.domain: Agentic virtual-cell perturbation experiments (E. coli gene knockout growth, yeast deletion fitness, K562 genetic-perturbation expression response)

repo_links.label: GitHub (first-author account; not cited in the preprint)

records.inputs: Natural-language biological questions or structured experiment requests naming the cell system, perturbation and readout
records.outputs: Predictions from registered task-specific models or structured abstention, with run reports, execution traces and provenance records
records.notes: Framework from Shandong University (Zhenyu Ma, Xukai Jiang) that sorts virtual-cell data, models, perturbations, adapters and validation evidence into one runtime. Agents parse questions, route data and models and build virtual experiments, while numbers come only from registered predictors and unsupported requests get structured abstention. Closure is in silico only, with no laboratory loop. Reported agreement is modest (median condition-level Spearman rho about 0.22 on a microbial benchmark). The code is MIT-licensed, but large datasets, trained assets and the full microbial benchmark pipelines are not packaged, and the preprint itself does not link the repository. Unrelated to the protein-engineering PRAXIS (asa-praxis).

records.name: TrialAtlas
records.domain: Clinical development planning: trial design deficiency detection, protocol optimisation and technical/regulatory success prediction
records.inputs: A structured clinical trial design description, plus ClinicalTrials.gov, PubMed/PubTator and openFDA (complete response letters, Drugs@FDA, labels) retrieved by tools
records.outputs: Design-deficiency assessments, recommended protocol optimisations and a binary regulatory-approval (technical and regulatory success) prediction, with structured outputs from each agent
records.notes: Memory-augmented multi-agent 'research organization' from UIUC and Keiji AI (Jimeng Sun group). A Director agent coordinates competing-trial, literature-synthesis and drug-benchmarking departments, whose working agents call domain APIs and a Docker code sandbox and draw on a memory of regulatory precedent. It was evaluated on TrialAtlasBench (from 291 FDA complete response letters; 36/35/104 items across three tasks), and experts judged 86.4% of generated concerns valid. The success prediction is a discrete label, not a calibrated probability. No prospective use is reported. The repository is public but has no licence file (README licence section is a TODO), while the benchmark data on Hugging Face are CC BY-4.0. The default backbone is GPT-5 via Azure OpenAI; the other supported backends are also commercial LLM APIs.

access_evidence.software_license: None: public repository with no licence file; README License section contains only a TODO placeholder at verification (2026-11-06). Benchmark data on Hugging Face: CC-BY-4.0

records.name: Genetic disease severity classification agent (HPO)
records.domain: Evidence-based severity classification of Human Phenotype Ontology terms and genes for reproductive genetic carrier screening
records.inputs: Lists of HPO term IDs, the HPO ontology file, ACMG-endorsed severity tiers and ACOG quality-of-life criteria, with PubMed/MeSH evidence retrieved through NCBI E-utilities
records.outputs: Per-term severity tiers, quality-of-life and management profiles with cited reasoning traces, LLM-based claim-support scores and gene-level severity tables
records.notes: ReAct plus retrieval-augmented agent (GPT-4o core model) from UNSW Sydney with University of Pittsburgh and other collaborators. It classified 10,211 HPO terms against ACMG and ACOG criteria, reporting 93.55% accuracy against expert-curated cohorts and 95.2% concordance with the Mackenzie's Mission gene list. Each term passes through contextualisation, query generation, PubMed retrieval, a conditional search expansion when evidence is sparse, and classification; a separate LLM agent then checks each cited claim and flagged 11.4% of classifications for human review. No experimental loop. The code is MIT-licensed and archived on Zenodo, but the public prompt is only a structural template: the production prompt is licensed to UNSW Sydney and available to reviewers or under an MTA, and the full per-term output is not redistributed, so the reported results cannot be fully reproduced from the open code.

records.name: PaleoRigor
records.domain: Bounded preparation of paleomicrobiome and ancient-DNA sequencing data for specialist analysis
records.inputs: A natural-language research request with uploaded metadata tables, sequencing files (FASTA/FASTQ), peptide tables or public repository accessions
records.outputs: A validated ordered workflow, checked and processed files, source-record comparisons, a report, and an exported run record with plan, intermediate files, checksums and any named refusal reason
records.notes: Huazhong University of Science and Technology (Ning lab) system, with University of Sydney and Yunnan University co-authors, delivered as macOS and Windows desktop applications that bundle seven local tools including Samtools, BWA and Bowtie 2. A language model (DeepSeek in the reported runs) drafts the workflow; a validator checks file references, formats and step dependencies, execution is limited to a fixed registry of local skills, and a planning contract makes the agent refuse out-of-scope requests with a named reason code. The paper describes expert checkpoints for plan review, run approval and result audit; the preregistered frozen evaluation (24 runs per model configuration, 23/24 and 24/24 passes) ran without the review step. It prepares data only: ancient-DNA authentication and biological interpretation stay with the paleobiologist. Source code is MIT; bundled third-party tools keep their own licences, several GPL-3.0.

records.name: EMET
records.domain: Preclinical drug-discovery research: disease biology, target identification and target-combination hypotheses
records.inputs: Scientist research questions and disease context; the platform has a proprietary biomedical knowledge graph of more than 1.5 billion triples linked to over 100 biological databases, plus models, tools and code execution
records.outputs: Ranked, mechanism-annotated target and target-combination hypotheses with retrieved evidence and provenance, kept in persistent memory across search rounds
records.notes: BenchSci's commercial, proprietary agentic research environment for preclinical R&D, offered as a hosted product with a free trial, a limited free academic tier and enterprise pilots. In a company-authored, non-peer-reviewed bioRxiv preprint, its Agentic Research Director, which BenchSci sells as the Hypothesis Generation Agent, ran multi-round graph-of-thoughts searches over the knowledge graph with link-prediction and retrieval tools and ranked two-target combinations for lung squamous cell carcinoma. The authors picked four combinations after internal vetting of the 20 top-ranked candidates. Pharmaron tested them in vitro under contract, using protocols the authors designed. Two of the four gave combination effects, including CDC7 plus PKMYT1 synergy in two cell lines. The system did not run the experiments; the lab-in-the-loop and self-driving-lab connectivity advertised on the product pages was not demonstrated in the study.

records.name: PEN-STACK
records.domain: Genome-writing design: insertion-site, writer-enzyme, cargo and delivery planning with off-target and biosecurity screening
records.inputs: A genome-writing goal and edit intent (free text resolved to a typed WriteSpec), target gene or locus, cell type and cargo size, sent through the CLI, Python SDK, MCP server or REST API, with any LLM as the optional driver
records.outputs: Ranked, cited site, writer, cargo and delivery write plans with calibrated confidence, per-mechanism off-target screens, biosecurity verdicts, scope ledgers and draft protocols that are never auto-run
records.notes: Open tool layer and co-scientist agent for genome-writing design, by Anees Ahmed Mahaboob Ali, Radhakrishnan Delhibabu and Everette Jacob Remington Nelson (all Vellore Institute of Technology). MIT-licensed, distributed on GitHub, PyPI (0.2.0) and Zenodo (concept DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21787136). It exposes ten design stages as twenty-two scope-aware tools over an SDK, an MCP server and a REST API, under an invariant that every reported quantity must come from a validated tool rather than a language model. In the preprint, three model families without tools supplied unsourced values for 90.8-98.8% of 240 required quantities, and supplied none when driving the tools; the grounded arm was only a four-goal audit, and eight of ten pre-registered claims did not pass (reported as machine-readable flags). The expression-robustness axis validated at exact-site resolution but not at the coarser default resolution. The design-build-test-learn loop runs in silico against a simulated lab and pauses for human approval at the safety, build and belief-admission gates; protocols are drafts and no physical experiment was run (autonomy level 3 on the Beal and Rogers scale, per docs/autonomy.md and the paper). The companion BioFirewall biosecurity middleware (arXiv 2608.20413; Apache-2.0 repository) is a governance component, not a separate row. Young single-group project, 3 GitHub stars at review, no external adopters reported in the paper.

decisions.name: Chaperone (agentic protein design harness)
decisions.rationale: New in-window system (bioRxiv 20 Oct 2026) from the Institute for Protein Design and HHMI at the University of Washington, corresponding author David Baker. Chaperone is a block-API harness that makes RFdiffusion3, ProteinMPNN, AlphaFold3 and more than 50 other protein-design tools interoperable for agents, with parallel execution on HPC. Multi-step scientific work is in scope: in the reported evaluation agents were given a design specification, GPUs and 12 hours to autonomously develop, execute, evaluate and refine design strategies, then submit 96 candidates scored by held-out pipelines. Code is public under a confirmed MIT licence, so access is open-source. No name, alias or URL match in the baseline (the only 'chaperone' sense in the catalog is biological, not a system name), so the record is named with a qualifier to prevent a future collision.

identity.note: Preprint resolves (HTTP 200) at https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898/2026.10.19.759896v1 , titled 'Reliable and Efficient Agentic Protein Design with Toolset Harnessing', v1 posted 20 Oct 2026, CC BY 4.0, no withdrawal notice and no newer version shown. Authors include Jasper Butcher, Jie Chen, Andrew Hunt, ... Neil P. King and David Baker (corresponding, dabaker@uw.edu); affiliations Institute for Protein Design / several UW departments / HHMI, plus FutureHouse, Google and SUSTech. Repository is official both ways: the paper's availability statement names github.com/RosettaCommons/chaperone and the repo README links back to this preprint. GitHub API: created 2026-10-12, pushed 2026-10-28, not archived, 163 stars, homepage rosettacommons.github.io/chaperone. No collision in the baseline: no 'chaperone' name/alias/normalized/URL match in asa_identity.tsv and none in asa_deprecated_ids.json; the nearest biology records (asa-praxis, asa-autoproteinengine, asa-agenticai-cross-tissue-protein-co-abundance-pipeline) are different systems with different papers and repos, and the existing '*Harness' records (asa-aido-harness, asa-arche, asa-ark) are unrelated. The name qualifier is justified: 'chaperone' is an ordinary biological term, so a future collision is plausible.

scope.note: In scope on two independent grounds. (1) It is a harness for multi-step scientific work: blocks for design, sequence design, folding and analysis (RFD3/RFD2, BindCraft, BoltzGen, ProteinMPNN variants, AF3, RF3, Boltz2, Chai1, OpenFold3, ESMFold2, plus RMSD/Foldseek/RASA/contact and H-bond metrics), with SLURM orchestration, chunking and path tracking, and shipped agent skills (SKILL.md, AGENTS.md, .agents/skills) for Claude Code and Codex. (2) The paper reports an agent benchmark with tasks and a held-out scoring function. Not a base model, not a general deep-research writer, not a one-off case study. The closest refutation I tried — 'this is only a scientific software component / interoperability library' — does not hold, because the agent-facing skill layer and the benchmark with held-out oracles are part of the released artifact, and catalog precedent keeps comparable orchestration harnesses in their domain category (asa-arche 'Arche-Harness', asa-cp-agent 'harness-cp-agents').

autonomy.note: A3 is supported and is the conservative reading. Observed closure: in the benchmark 'agents were required to submit 96 sequence-diverse candidate designs' and were allowed '12 hours and access to GPUs to autonomously develop, execute, evaluate, ...' their strategies, scored by 'held-out scoring pipelines' not visible to the agent. That is tool-using workflow closure in silico only. A4 would be overstated: in the cortisol campaign the agent ran 104 small-scale runs 'under designer guidance' and a researcher selected 10 backbone configurations, and the paper describes designer guidance and researcher selection at several stages. A5 is correctly not claimed: the wet-lab work (yeast surface display screening, fluorescence polarization in 96-well plates) was done by human authors, so no physical loop is closed by the system. B is correctly not used: the harness is the primary artifact, the benchmark is one component.

access.note: open-source is confirmed, not inferred. GitHub API repos/RosettaCommons/chaperone reports license spdx_id MIT, and repos/RosettaCommons/chaperone/license resolves to path LICENSE / MIT. The raw file https://raw.githubusercontent.com/RosettaCommons/chaperone/main/LICENSE returned HTTP 200 and begins 'MIT License' / 'Copyright (c) 2025 The Chaperone Authors'. THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md in the repo states the MIT project licence does not replace terms attached to bundled third-party code, external tools, model weights or databases, and the README notes some tools or weights need a separate upstream download or access agreement — the proposed notes already say this, which is the right treatment (the record's own access reflects the harness code, not the orchestrated backends). access_evidence null is acceptable because the licence is a plain MIT file.

category.note: biology is correct: protein design / structural biology tooling. 'benchmark' would be wrong because the released artifact is the harness; chemistry would be wrong because the tasks are protein (small-molecule binder, nanoparticle, DNA-binder) design rather than synthesis. Consistent with asa-praxis and asa-autoproteinengine being filed under biology.

urls.note: All four URLs in the proposal were fetched by me in this task and support their labels: biorxiv v1 landing page (200, title/date/licence), biorxiv v1 .full (200, benchmark design, cortisol results, availability statement), github.com/RosettaCommons/chaperone (200 via curl and via authenticated GitHub API, description and contents), raw LICENSE (200, MIT). No constructed or completed URL in the record.

text.note: Two factual corrections needed in notes, both in the direction of less autonomy. (a) The cortisol campaign is described in a way that reads as agent-driven; the paper states the computational stage ran 'under designer guidance' with a researcher selecting 10 of 104 backbone configurations, and the explicit screening criterion was human-set ('Designs with estimated apparent KD values <=1 uM were classified as candidate binders'). (b) The two-week figure in the paper covers going 'from initial design hypotheses to sequences ready for experimental testing', not the whole campaign including assays; the proposal's phrasing ('a two-week campaign produced low-nanomolar cortisol binders') compresses this. Also worth fixing for precision: the benchmark was run with GPT-5.6 Sol through Codex against a standard Codex baseline (so the efficiency numbers are agent-specific, not general); 15 of 27 FP-tested designs gave supported fits; and the repo README states 'over 80 blocks' in the registry while the abstract says 'more than 50 other protein design tools', so the record should keep the paper's figure and not inflate it. Everything else in notes/inputs/outputs traces to the sources I fetched.

decisions.name: CryoPilot
decisions.rationale: New in-window system (bioRxiv 30 Oct 2026) from the Kihara Lab at Purdue University. Two language-model agents carry single-particle cryo-EM data from micrographs to validated atomic models: the reconstruction agent chooses and parameterises CryoSPARC jobs, tests alternatives and reverts decisions, and the modelling agent builds and trims models with CryoZeta, DAQ, Phenix and Rosetta. That is multi-step scientific work with tool execution and analysis, in scope. The preprint says only that a binary 'will be available'; the official site now serves an installer and states PolyForm Noncommercial 1.0.0 terms, so the artifact exists today but is a non-commercial binary rather than open source, hence source-available with access evidence. No baseline name, alias or URL match.

The authors are Punuru, Klose and Kihara (Purdue). The preprint's own Data and code availability statement names https://cryopilot.vercel.app/, so the site is author-endorsed; the site footer reads 'Kihara Lab, Purdue University' and its binary is served from kiharalab.org. There is no baseline duplicate. The nearest baseline record, asa-cryoagent (Fei Sun lab, 'cryoAgent: An agentic workflow for robust and adaptive end-to-end cryo-EM image processing', bioRxiv 2026.04.16.718662), is a different system with different authors. SAME-NAME COLLISION, not flagged in the proposal: github.com/ZishanShu/CryoPilot (created 2026-04-19, no licence, no paper link) is an unrelated RELION-based cryo-EM agent project whose repo description reads 'CryoAgent: Towards Autonomous Cryo-EM Structure Determination...'. It must never be linked to this record.

scope.note: Multi-step scientific work with tool execution. A reconstruction agent selects and parameterises CryoSPARC jobs, inspects class averages and diagnostics, and revises or reverts its own decisions. A modelling agent fixes handedness, builds models with CryoZeta, trims regions without density support and refines with Phenix/Rosetta against map fit, geometry and DAQ. It is not a base model, a deep-research writer or a single software component.

autonomy.note: A3-A4 is supported as in-silico closure: data go end to end from micrographs to refined models. This is computational only, so A5 does not apply. Human involvement that must be disclosed: the preprint says that, except in two cases where the authors revised the goal statement or the particle-picking strategy after an initial run, the only human inputs were the data, acquisition information and a short goal. The alpha-latrocrustotoxin map reached 4.15 A only after an author-suggested picking strategy; the first run reached 5.9 A. The abstract says 'minimal human intervention'. All eight modelling runs proceeded without human intervention. The proposed notes omit the two human revisions.

access.note: The licence is confirmed: the official site says 'Free for noncommercial use under the PolyForm Noncommercial License 1.0.0', and the changelog dates the PolyForm NC release to 0.2.0 (2026-10-27). The licence is accepted in-app at first start. Commercial use requires contacting D. Kihara. Distribution is a single Linux x86_64 binary (v0.3.5, 2026-11-04). A HEAD request on the kiharalab.org binary returns 200 with about 294 MB; it was not downloaded. No public source code was found, and the only same-name GitHub repo is unrelated. Under the task's rule (restrictive/NC licence -> source-available), 'source-available' is the nearest bucket, but this is a binary-only release. access_evidence must say explicitly that no source code is public, so the label is not read as 'code inspectable'. Further dependencies: proprietary CryoSPARC v5 (separately licensed, Structura), an OpenAI or Anthropic API key, a CryoZeta account (em.kiharalab.org) for building from sequence, and PyMOL/ChimeraX (Phenix/Rosetta optional). The installer reports installs to the site by default, with a documented opt-out.

category.note: biology: structural biology, cryo-EM reconstruction and atomic model building. This matches the precedent of asa-cryoagent (biology).

urls.note: All proposed URLs return HTTP 200 and support their labels: the bioRxiv v1 landing page; the JATS source XML (an auxiliary source, not a display link); and https://cryopilot.vercel.app/ (official site and download, author-endorsed in the preprint). The instructions and changelog pages also return 200. Do not add github.com/ZishanShu/CryoPilot.

text.note: Two errors in the notes. (1) 'EMPIAR-10025 was used to develop the instructions and is therefore not a held-out test' implies EMPIAR-10025 is among the nine evaluation datasets. The preprint says it was EXCLUDED from evaluation; it is the modelling agent that was developed in earlier runs on maps from this study. (2) The two author interventions (revised goal statement or picking strategy) are not disclosed. Also add: seven refined models agreed with reference structures within 0.4-4.9 A Calpha RMSD. Both agents used GPT-5.5 in the paper; Claude models were added in later releases (0.3.0-0.3.4). Other figures check out against the preprint: eight of nine reconstructions at 2.61-3.51 A, eight modelling runs without human intervention in 2.6-10.8 h. The inputs field should also mention CryoSPARC credentials and the optional sequence.

decisions.name: GENIE (closed-loop autonomous microscopy)
decisions.rationale: New in-window system (bioRxiv 13 Oct 2026) from the Laufer Center and Department of Biochemistry and Cell Biology at Stony Brook University. GENIE takes one plain-language goal and closes the loop on a real light microscope: a fixed five-stage controller plans, screens each instruction through a deterministic safety gate, drives the instrument through a hardware layer, interprets returned images and writes its own analysis, ending in a statistically tested answer. This is an actually demonstrated physical laboratory loop in biology (live-cell mitochondrial membrane-potential measurement, plus a transfer run on a second microscope with different hardware), which is the case the catalog admits as paper-only. The code is explicitly not released, and the figure-level data are on Zenodo under CC BY-NC-ND, so access is paper-only. No baseline name or URL match; the existing TrialGenie, ToolsGenie 2.0 and PromptGenie records are different systems, so the record carries a qualifier.

autonomy.note: A5 alone overstates observed closure; correct to A4-A5 (catalog precedent for instrument-operation agents: MicroClaw A3-A5, TEM Agent A3-A5, Agentic AFM A3-A5). The physical loop is real (GENIE drove two microscopes directly through its own hardware layer, flagged defocused fields and refocused, set the illuminated field), but adaptivity during acquisition was narrow: the prompt fixed channels, region, replicate count, illumination powers and exposures, and required acquisition to start before any pilot image or analysis; all four dishes were acquired before analysis, so results never fed back into new acquisition (authors list choosing discriminating measurements as future work). Human/agent inputs disclosed in the paper: an operator loaded each dish, the run directory was copied to a separate computer for analysis, the operator gave 7 inputs (settings update raising token limits, pixel-size confirmation, API budget, close), and a watcher LLM supplied 54 hints that became standing constraints. Ran at four of seven autonomy levels behind a deterministic, model-free gate.

scope.note: Borderline but passes. The core is a perturbation-response predictor (knowledge compile -> embed -> train -> predict -> generate). The agentic part is Explain, where an LLM answers source-grounded questions, tools check citations and paths, and answers that fail the checks are revised. This is comparable to the catalogued GeneAgent (A2, self-verifying gene-set agent), so it is not merely a base model or software component. identity.note: arXiv:2610.16975 resolves (HTTP 200), title 'MADDIE: Multi-Agent Drug Discovery Engine', authors Ye Liu, Reza Averly, Avery Meyer, Frazier N. Baker, Ruoxi Gao, Daniel Adu-Ampratwum, Xia Ning (The Ohio State University, emails @osu.edu in the HTML author block). Submission history v1 2026-10-12, v2 2026-10-20, v3 2026-10-21; no withdrawal or comment notice. The abstract itself links github.com/ninglab/MADDIE, so the repo is author-endorsed; repo README carries the arXiv badge and the matching citation block. Not a duplicate or rename of a baseline record: asa-liddia (ninglab/LIDDiA) and asa-madd (Solovev et al., arXiv 2511.08217) are both cited BY this paper as prior/baseline systems, and asa-larc (ninglab/LARC) is a different task. Near-collision MADD vs MADDIE is real and both are chemistry drug-discovery multi-agent systems from different groups - disambiguated in notes.

scope.note: In scope. Multi-step scientific work with real tool execution: Orchestrator plans and re-plans over four worker agents wrapping third-party scientific tools (conDitar/DiffSMol generation, GeLLMO-C and 11 MolOpt optimizers, MEEA* retrosynthesis and PrexSyn, Uni-Dock docking, ADMET-AI, Lilly MedChem rules, QED/SAScore). Not a base model, not a general deep-research writer, not a one-off case study, not a software component - the bundled tools are components, the engine orchestrating them is the system. Evaluated across 50 protein targets with a benchmark harness in tests/.

autonomy.note: A3-A4 is supported and is the ceiling. Observed closure: campaign runs to a self-determined stop (Orchestrator's own stop decision, or the <POOL=N> count of molecules passing every property and having a synthesis route, or exhaustion of the --max_iter action budget, default 100); flexible non-linear workflow rather than a fixed pipeline, with episodic and semantic memory. NOT A5: all closure is in silico. The paper's Discussion states in vitro work is a future step - 'both synthesis and in vitro experimentation remain challenging to perform systematically and at scale' - and human-in-the-loop is explicitly described as a future extension, not what was run. scope.note: In scope. Not a base model, not a general report writer, not a single software component: the paper describes a fixed orchestration of LLM stages that reads a curated literature corpus, picks a disease/design intent, selects a target and a PDB structure, chooses hotspot residues, then generates and folds candidate binders with external design and folding tools and reports the campaign. That is multi-step scientific work with tool execution across literature, hypothesis (target/epitope choice), in-silico experiment and reporting. Three end-to-end campaigns are reported (CALCRL/RAMP1, PD-1/PD-L1, PVR-TIGIT). The database ablation (41/48 vs 0/48 test questions) is an internal evaluation, not a benchmark record, so 'biology' rather than 'benchmark' is right.

autonomy.note: A3-A4 is supported and the ceiling is correct. Observed closure is in-silico only: the paper states it has not evaluated experimental success and offers in-silico metrics as a proxy, so A5 is excluded (no physical loop, and the catalog rule already excludes simulation closure). Workflow orchestration is fixed by design (12-stage orchestrator per the repository README), which is A3; the autonomous choice of design intent, target, structure and hotspots from a single prompt, plus one run raising its own iPTM threshold after a high calibration hit rate, reaches toward A4. CORRECTION REQUIRED under MAINTENANCE.md line 11 ('Human safety gates ... must be disclosed'): the proposed notes disclose no gates, but the full text describes three — the pipeline pauses for a user-supplied structure when none is found, it stops and prints options to the user when calibration returns ITERATE, and stages stop when a safety classifier triggers. These must appear in the notes.

decisions.name: PharmAgents2
decisions.rationale: New in-window system (arXiv 2611.07653, submitted 5 Nov 2026) from AIPher Technology with the Institute for AI Industry Research at Tsinghua University: the successor to the catalogued PharmAgents (asa-pharmagents, arXiv:2503.22164), with a different architecture (Paper2Skill decision knowledge plus Self-Scaling Discovery parallel agents) and its own benchmark. Following the AI Scientist / AI Scientist-v2 precedent this is a separate record rather than a match. No code, benchmark package or platform release was found, so it is paper-only; admitted despite that because three real-world investigations produced findings that human researchers then confirmed experimentally, including a previously unreported LpxH allosteric site with a novel inhibitor scaffold and a new binding target for a known bioactive molecule. Orchestrator: paper-only without agent-run physical closure (compounds were purchased and tested by researchers); the paper-only exception is reserved for demonstrated lab closure or a deployed institutional system. Reconsider when code or a platform is released.

Affiliations in HTML: AIPher Technology; Institute for AI Industry Research (AIR), Tsinghua University. Not a duplicate of asa-pharmagents (arXiv:2503.22164, 'PharmAgents: Building a Virtual Pharma...'): different paper, architecture (Paper2Skill, Self-Scaling Discovery, AIPherDD platform) and benchmark; separate record is consistent with the AI Scientist / AI Scientist-v2 precedent. Successor relation is INFERRED, not stated: 5 shared authors (Bowen Gao, Wenxuan Xie, Ya-Qin Zhang, Wei-Ying Ma, Yanyan Lan) and the name, but my text search of the PharmAgents2 HTML found no citation of or reference to the original PharmAgents paper. No same-name collision with baseline (only asa-pharmagents, asa-pharmaswarm, asa-talk2biomodels match 'pharm'); unrelated GitHub repos named PharmAgent/pharmagents_* exist (SXY-xinyun/PharmAgent, nahaltaurus/pharmagents_project, Melody-1128/pharmagents-scholar-service) and are not affiliated; none should be linked.

scope.note: Multi-step in-silico drug discovery agent: hypothesis generation (allosteric site, covalent strategy, proteome-wide target ranking), tool execution on the AIPherDD platform, reviewer-agent revision, candidate nomination and reports. Not a base model, deep-research writer or component. Includes its own benchmark (PharmAgents-Bench v0.1) but the record is the system, so category biology is right, not benchmark.

autonomy.note: A4 supported for in-silico closure: humans specified target and objective only ('They left the binding pocket, proposed mechanism, and screening protocol open'), the system planned and ran computational investigations and delivered candidates. No physical loop: 'researchers purchased and tested the nominated compounds'; all wet-lab work human-executed, so A5 correctly NOT claimed. A3-A4 (as for PharmAgents v1) would also be defensible; A4 accepted given autonomous hypothesis generation and plan revision.

access.note: paper-only correct: no code, benchmark package or public platform. HTML contains no project/code URLs besides arXiv/LaTeXML boilerplate; gh search repos 'PharmAgents' and 'AIPher' found no official repo; one WebSearch found no release (a Dealroom company profile, lead only, describes AIPher as a Tsinghua AIR spin-out building on PharmAgents). AIPherDD is described as a supporting platform but no public access was found, so platform is not justified. Paper licence is CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 (paper only, not software). Significance for a paper-only ADD is borderline but acceptable: major institutional group (Tsinghua AIR, 25 authors) with three documented real-world uses whose nominated compounds/targets received human wet-lab testing (63 LpxH and 34 JAK1 compounds purchased and tested; SPR binding for target ranking). HOLD would also be defensible under the default rule; catalog precedent (asa-pharmagents and ~60 other paper-only records) favours ADD.

(5) The end-to-end comparison was against Claude Code, Codex and LLM-only all on a DeepSeek base model; 'highest process scores on all three end-to-end tasks' matches the abstract but is the authors' own benchmark.

The README still cites the v1 title. Same authors (Liu ... Ogata, Zhu). The paper's Code availability statement names github.com/ZhuGroup-GT/GBClaw, and the org is 'Zhu Research Group at Georgia Tech' (Ting Zhu, last/corresponding author), so the repo is official. The repo is not a fork; tags v1.0 and v1.1 exist and there are no GitHub releases. No baseline record is named GBClaw. The other *Claw records (MatClaw, MolClaw, Claw AI Lab, Dr. Claw, ScienceClaw, MicroClaw, MetaClaw, AutoResearchClaw) are different systems, and the paper cites MatClaw as separate prior work. No collision.

scope.note: In scope: an orchestrator plus five specialist agents plan, build bicrystals, run LAMMPS (relaxation, GB energy, shear, NEB), analyse with OVITO and custom code, and replan. It was applied to 14 Ni asymmetric tilt GBs with new mechanistic findings. It is not a base model, a deep-research writer or a plain software component.

autonomy.note: A3 is supported. The paper describes a 'human-in-the-loop agentic framework', and the code has an approve_project_plan_draft tool. Follow-up studies were 'researcher-guided', and researcher guidance prompted the HRTEM automation. Closure is computational only. The paper says agents for experimental validation are 'currently under development', so A5 does not apply. A4 is not supported because researchers set the objectives and approve the plans.

access.note: open-source confirmed. GitHub API license spdx_id is MIT and the LICENSE file is 'MIT License, Copyright (c) 2026 Yazhuo Liu'. The paper's Code availability statement says MIT. Third-party runtimes (LAMMPS, OVITO, potentials, LLM provider) keep their own terms, which the notes already say.

category.note: Correct to physics. The science is defect mechanics and deformation of metal grain boundaries (misfit dislocations, sliding, shear strength). That is materials physics/mechanics from a mechanical-engineering group (cond-mat.mtrl-sci). The catalog maps materials-physics/engineering to physics (MechAgents, AutoMOOSE microstructure simulation, TritonDFT). Counter-precedent: LAMMPS-Agents and AtomAgents (general LAMMPS materials-property and alloy design) sit in chemistry, so this is a curator judgment. If the curator prefers the tool-based precedent (LAMMPS -> chemistry), reverting is low-risk.

identity.note: arXiv 2610.34203 resolves (HTTP 200), title 'MatOS: An Agent Operating System for Materials Research', submitted 25 Oct 2026, v1 only; Comments field reads '54 pages, 21 figures, 11 tables' with no withdrawal notice. Abstract links https://github.com/DingyangLyu/MatOS; the repo owner is the first author, whom the paper credits as the main implementer. Repo created 2026-10-25, not a fork, README cites the Zhongguancun Academy technical report. No MatOS / Zhongguancun / 'agent operating system' entry in asa_identity.tsv or asa_deprecated_ids.json. Nearby baseline records (MatClaw, MIRA, ResearchClawBench) are distinct systems that the paper cites as related work. No same-name collision found in the baseline.

scope.note: This is an agent runtime that carries out multi-step computational materials research: asset graph, stateful workflow with Exec/Backend/Guard nodes, and asset evolution. It is evaluated end to end on ResearchClawBench, where the system must 'execute experiments and computations, and write a research report', and on MatTools and SciAgentGym. It is not a base model, deep-research writer or library.

autonomy.note: A3-A4 is supported. A4 rests on the ResearchClawBench end-to-end in-silico runs. The eight research cases are researcher-led: the Contributors section says Hongwei Du 'carried out six of the eight research cases', and the method cases say 'Using MatOS for strategy development ... we developed'. That evidence fits A3. Closure is computational only (MD, DFT, surrogate models). The README roadmap leaves 'Connect instruments and experimental protocols' unticked, so A5 does not apply. Human gates should be disclosed: Human decision nodes and human confirmation in the workflow runtime, and asset evolution set to manual approval by default in the workspace profile.

access.note: The LICENSE file reads 'PolyForm Noncommercial License 1.0.0'. The GitHub API reports the licence as 'other' / NOASSERTION. LICENSING.md says 'Commercial use is not permitted'. Bundled third-party parts (DeepSeek Harness MIT, OpenDesign Apache-2.0, MatterViz MIT) keep their own licences. The correct access value is source-available with access_evidence, as proposed. The public repo is 'the open, single-user MatOS edition' with a 37-asset workspace profile, a subset of the larger asset library described in the paper (e.g. 65 knowledge assets). The notes should say so.

category.note: chemistry matches catalog precedent for computational materials agents (VASPilot, MatClaw, DREAMS, LLaMP are chemistry). physics would also be defensible: TritonDFT, and the CFD case in the appendix. Keep chemistry.

urls.note: All four URLs fetched: the arXiv abs and HTML pages, the GitHub repo and the LICENSE blob each returned HTTP 200 and support their labels.

text.note: The proposed notes credit the case results to MatOS as if it produced them autonomously ('eight computational research cases, including narrowing over 30 million structures'). The paper's contributor statement shows researchers carried out the cases with MatOS. Several case figures are 'Adapted from Du et al.' (prior work by a co-author), and the screening uses 'the hierarchical framework of Du et al.'. The notes also omit that the public repo is a reduced single-user edition and do not disclose the human gates. Benchmark gains were measured on a single base model per comparison (DeepSeek-V4-Flash/Pro). Notes rewritten in corrected_record. Inputs and outputs are factual, with a minor tweak.

identity.note: arXiv 2610.23839 resolves (HTTP 200), title 'DiscoveryRSI: Recursively Learning to Discover Valuable Hypotheses', v1 2026-10-16, v2 2026-10-20, no withdrawal notice. The abs page Code link points to github.com/Gen-Verse/DiscoveryRSI, whose homepage field points back to the arXiv paper, so the repo is author-endorsed. The README links the HF model, HF dataset and DFM-Bench. Baseline check: the only other Gen-Verse record is asa-sciencebuddy (a different system, arXiv 2609.17523). No DiscoveryRSI/DFM-Bench entry in asa_identity.tsv. Name-similar baseline records (DiscoveryWorld, DiscoveryBench, BioDiscoveryAgent, Microsoft Discovery, SwarmRSI held in the same lane) are different systems, so there is no collision. Minor: the README BibTeX lists an extra author (James Zou) who is not on the arXiv author list. This does not affect the record.

scope.note: In scope: a multi-agent system (Lead/Generation/Evolution/Critique/Progress/Compiler roles) that develops hypothesis trees and investigation plans and compiles selected computational plans into Harbor tasks with inputs, environments and verification checks, plus the DFM-Bench evaluation protocol. Hypothesis development is listed scientific work. It is not a general deep-research writer. Borderline flag: much of the paper is about training a model (DiscoveryRSI-27B, fine-tuned from Qwen3.8-27B). The record should be framed as the hypothesis-development system, not as a model release.

autonomy.note: A2-A3 is supported, and the upper bound should stay at A3. The paper reports generation, critique, selection and compilation, but not execution of the compiled investigations. It says learning experience is gathered 'before a complete investigation has been executed', and it leaves execution (e.g. via RSI-Anything) and wet-lab validation to future work. The public harness is only a propose/critique/select loop with three stub tools (record_evidence, compare, falsify), which puts the released code at A2. No physical loop, so A5 does not apply.

access.note: The open-source label is supported for the DiscoveryRSI repo. The LICENSE file (178 bytes) reads 'Apache License 2.0 / Copyright 2026 Gen-Verse / Licensed under the Apache License, Version 2.0', and the README says 'Project-owned code is licensed under Apache-2.0'. GitHub reports NOASSERTION because the file holds a grant notice rather than the full licence text. The HF model (LICENSE file holds the full Apache-2.0 text; card states it is inherited from the Qwen3.8-27B base) and the HF dataset are tagged apache-2.0, public and not gated. CORRECTIONS: (a) DFM-Bench (github.com/Gen-Verse/DFM-Bench) has NO licence. GitHub returns license null, the /license endpoint returns 404, and no licence statement was found in its README or pyproject. It is therefore source-available and must be disclosed in access_evidence, not shown as if covered by the open-source label. (b) The public DiscoveryRSI code is a thin harness of about 24 KB of Python (pyproject: 'A small, model-agnostic agentic system'). It does not contain the paper's evolutionary search operators, Harbor compiler, hypothesis-credit-optimization training or harness-replay pipeline. The open-source label applies to that reduced harness plus the open weights, and the notes should say so.

category.note: biology is correct. The paper evaluates four life-science domains (clinical/population health, therapeutic-target prioritization, disease mechanisms, population multi-omics) using HCC cohort, MIMIC-IV, eICU, UK Biobank, GEO and ArrayExpress data. The README says 'DiscoveryRSI focuses on life-science research'. The battery setting is only a DFM-Bench extension and does not justify crossdomain.

urls.note: All proposed URLs fetched with HTTP 200: arXiv abs, GitHub DiscoveryRSI, raw LICENSE, HF model, HF dataset, GitHub DFM-Bench. Each supports its label. The DFM-Bench link needs an access caveat because that repo is unlicensed.

text.note: Three corrections are needed. (1) outputs presents 'investigations compiled as executable Harbor tasks; DFM-Bench process scores' as what the system delivers. The public harness has no Harbor compiler: role_compiler.md is a 240-byte prompt, and the only Harbor material is three example task packages on HF. Attribute Harbor compilation to the paper's pipeline. (2) The 6.3% figure is an author-reported retrospective 'literature-inspiration' measure against papers published after each model's cutoff, and the README calls it an 'actionable-reference rate'. Keep it labelled as author-reported and avoid implying discovery. (3) The notes say project code is Apache-2.0 without saying that DFM-Bench is unlicensed or that the public harness is a reduced version of the paper's system. The other statements were checked against the paper and README: 4.86 to 5.39, preliminary human assessment, no execution reported, no patient data bundled.

scope.note: Multi-step physical experimental science: from a campaign brief the agent chooses recipes, runs cryogenic transport sweeps on real devices, analyses data and returns a conclusion (stacking order; superconductivity). Not a base model, deep-research writer, case study or component.

autonomy.note: A5 supported by observed closure on real hardware. In mode E1 'the agent executes the measurement cells it writes' on the rig control computer; blinded prospective trial on two multilayer graphene devices matched the expert's sealed conclusions; tetralayer session ran with no operator intervention; domain transfer (WSe2-proximitized bilayer graphene, second rig) found superconductivity autonomously, but only after a few hours of expert protocol writing and two protocol corrections (Table S5: E1 sessions, one session ended by the operator). Human gates that must be disclosed: operator runs setup and safety cells and grants autonomy by a named phrase; device-card safety limits are enforced in the instrument layer and the agent never changes them; brief lists consent-required and banned operations; agent drops to human-in-the-loop (E0) on any safety concern (device 1 waited 11.4 h overnight for an operator ruling on gate leakage); every corpus revision is accepted/rejected by a human. Proposed notes mention goals/boundaries, safety limits and interventions but omit the explicit autonomy grant and the E0 fallback; added in correction.

autonomy.note: A4 overstates observed closure; A3-A4 is the defensible reading. Catalog precedent for in-silico frameworks with essential human steering is A3-A4 (Ansatz, GoalEvolve, VALG).

identity.note: arXiv:2610.21118 v1 (15 Oct 2026, hep-ph) resolves (HTTP 200); title 'PTagent: An LLM-assisted tool for finite-temperature model construction in cosmological phase transitions'; authors Lei Wu, Yang Xiao, Jin Min Yang, Yang Zhang; comments '17 pages, 3 figures'; no withdrawal notice. Repo github.com/Contract-Mediated-Agent/PTagent is named in the paper's Quick Start section (author-endorsed); org created 2026-06-22, not a fork, not archived. No baseline match by name/URL/arXiv ID; not in deprecated IDs. Distinct from baseline asa-darkagents (DarkAgents / DarkAgent-PT, arXiv:2606.11157, PhysicsZandi repo), which the PTagent paper cites as separate prior work, and from asa-lewron (paper-only EWPT system).

scope.note: Borderline but in scope by catalog precedent (HEPLocalAgent, SMEFT-Pheno-Agent, DarkAgents). Multi-step scientific workflow: reads a SARAH model, arXiv paper or DRalgo source, extracts and organizes model expressions, derives thermal self-energies with consistency checks, flags unresolved physical choices, assembles a reviewable model contract with provenance graph, then generates CosmoTransitions/PhaseTracer numerical potentials and (in the paper's examples) runs the transition calculation. Not a base model, deep-research writer or case study. Risk to note: its stated primary purpose is model construction, so it is close to a domain software component; the agentic paper-to-model interpretation step keeps it above that line.

autonomy.note: A2-A3 supported. Observed closure: agent-driven interpretation plus deterministic backend execution, with a mandatory human review/approval gate on the model specification before numerical generation (disclosed in abstract and Sec. 2). No autonomous hypothesis generation or result interpretation; no physical loop. Tested with three LLM backends on the paper's three examples.

access.note: open-source confirmed: GitHub license endpoint returns path LICENSE, spdx GPL-3.0; LICENSE file first line 'GNU GENERAL PUBLIC LICENSE Version 3, 29 June 2007'. No releases published (code on default branch only). External dependencies (SARAH, Wolfram/Mathematica for SARAH/DRalgo routes, PhaseTracer) are not bundled; README states no LLM API key is needed beyond the host agent environment.

category.note: physics (hep-ph / cosmology) consistent with HEP agents in baseline.

urls.note: All four URLs fetched: arXiv abs 200, arXiv HTML 200 (contains repo link), GitHub repo page 200, GitHub license API 200 (GPL-3.0). Each supports its label.

text.note: Proposed notes say PTagent 'does not itself run phase-transition analyses'. The paper contradicts this: in both Quick Start examples, after approval 'the dedicated backend generates the CosmoTransitions implementation and runs the phase-transition calculation' (Sec. 2.1) and 'constructs the PhaseTracer implementation and runs the transition calculation' (Sec. 2.2). Corrected: it runs the downstream calculation via external codes but its stated purpose is model construction and it does not interpret results. Inputs: add DeepSeek Harness as a second documented host environment; note SARAH/Mathematica/DRalgo/PhaseTracer dependencies.

scope.note: Reusable workflow package: AGENTS.md protocol plus solver and validation tooling with which a general coding agent runs feasibility checks, writes configs, submits RCWA optimizations, applies an 11-point analysis checklist, queues FDTD cross-validation and proposes the next step. Precedent: asa-get-physics-done-gpd (A3, a protocol installed into general coding agents). This is not a base model, deep-research writer or bare software component; demonstrated on three case studies plus a transfer case (S12, quasi-BIC).

autonomy.note: A3 supported: the agent executes and analyses multi-stage simulation campaigns. A human gate must be disclosed. The paper says the agent 'asks for approval before computationally expensive runs'. The user starts the execution bridge and does all authentication, and the human review time for proposals was not recorded. AGENTS.md §5 ends each iteration by reporting 'one concrete next step' to the user. Simulation/HPC only, so not A5; A4 is not claimed or shown.

Kept in scope because the work is computational physics (fluids, elastic solids, rods, cloth, multiphysics) and the catalog already lists comparable physics-simulation agent benchmarks (SimulCost, PhysGym, both category benchmark, autonomy B). decisions.rationale: A licensed release now exists. Its README links Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.22135808 (CC-BY-4.0), a record titled exactly as the paper and authored by first author Xuerui Fang (Donghua University). The owner account's other repos (SchNarc, MANTA-LCT, LIGHT_platform) fit a computational-chemistry group. The paper's own code link could not be read because ChemRxiv is blocked, so ownership rests on the repo→Zenodo→first-author chain. Scope: a domain multi-agent system that does evidence-grounded QA and property-constrained polymer design with ML predictors. It is comparable to the catalogued Polymer-Agent (A2-A3) and is not a general deep-research tool. Closure is computational only.

scope.note: This is a domain multi-agent system with real multi-step tooling. Intent routing, a planner/executor, a quality-supervised RAG loop with question reformulation, and a design pipeline (design brief, idea generation, scoring, then ML property predictors in ML_Tool) are all present in the code, along with a report generator. It is not a general deep-research writer because it is tied to degradable-polymer corpora and trained property predictors. It is comparable to the displayed asa-polymer-agent. The case is borderline: Query Mode is essentially RAG QA. Design Mode, combined with the ML tools, is what puts it in scope.

autonomy.note: A2-A3 is supported. Code shows a bounded quality loop (max_attempts) and an LLM generate/score design pipeline, run interactively in a Streamlit chat. The abstract reports only retrieval, QA and design benchmarks, with no experimental or simulation closure, so the system does not reach A4 or A5.

decisions.name: MoSeS autonomous chromatography
decisions.rationale: Artifacts are now confirmed, but the licence and scope questions are still open. The MoSeS library is public on the Aspuru-Guzik group GitLab (created 2026-01-22, active 2026-10-21) and on PyPI as moses-hplc 1.0.0 (2026-08-27; authors match the paper). Licence is unconfirmed: pyproject.toml declares license = {file = "LICENSE"} and an MIT classifier, but the GitLab tree has no LICENSE file and GitLab detects no licence. The paper scripts repo fsk-lab/lcbo still has no licence (licence API 404); its paper data are on Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.22109729 (CC-BY-4.0). On scope, the abstract presents MoSeS as an instrument-control and data-processing software layer, with BO-driven autonomous method development and purification-method development as demonstrations. Non-LLM self-driving platforms are catalogued (Polybot, RoboChem-Flex), but whether this is an autonomous experimental system or a software component, and how far the physical loop ran without a human, needs the full text, which is still blocked.
decisions.reconsider_when: Either a LICENSE file is added to the GitLab moses repository (pyproject already points to one) or the licence is otherwise confirmed, AND the full text shows MoSeS running a closed physical loop (instrument run -> model update -> next run) without per-iteration human action. If both hold, add it as a chemistry A5 platform (lab-gated/open-source per the licence, following the Polybot/RoboChem-Flex precedent). If the full text frames it purely as a software toolbox, REJECT_SCOPE.

decisions.name: Qiushi Engine
decisions.rationale: The October hold looked only at the kissing-number paper. Today's check found the group's earlier preprint arXiv 2604.27092 (v1, not withdrawn, Zhejiang University corresponding authors Yihao Yang and Hongsheng Chen). In it, Qiushi (Discovery) Engine controls a real benchtop free-space optical platform (laser, SLM, power meter, two cameras) through program modules. It reproduces a transmission-matrix experiment and experimentally validates a proposed 'optical bilinear interaction' mechanism. That is a demonstrated physical-lab loop at a major institution, which meets the catalogue's paper-only bar even though the engine is still unreleased. The Zenodo deposit says explicitly that the core system and hardware-control software are not included. The Oxelra-AI repositories hold research outputs only (optical repo: no licence asserted; kissing-number repo: MIT software plus CC BY 4.0 content). So access is paper-only, not open-source. Not in the baseline under either name.
decisions.reconsider_when: Upgrade the access field if the Qiushi Engine core or hardware-control code is released, or Oxelra documents user access (platform). Recheck for journal publication of 2604.27092. Collision watch: Oxelra-AI also has BabyLM, Matmul and causality-sum-rules repositories run by the same engine; these are not separate systems.

identity.note: arXiv 2604.27092 (v1, 29 Apr 2026, 'End-to-end autonomous scientific discovery on a real optical platform') and 2609.35051 (v1, 28 Sep 2026, kissing-number constructions) both resolve; no withdrawal notice on either abs page. They share authors (Shuxing Yang, Hongsheng Chen, Yihao Yang). The PDF confirms Zhejiang University affiliations, with Yihao Yang and Hongsheng Chen as corresponding authors. The kissing-number repository is linked from the 2609.35051 arXiv comments field, so it is author-endorsed. The optical repository sits in the same Oxelra-AI org, lists the paper authors, and carries the Zenodo DOI. oxelra.com links github.com/orgs/Oxelra-AI and cites arXiv:2604.27092. The only baseline match is the held_lead row for this same system. OPERA (asa-opera, autonomous optical experiments, arXiv 2608.05990, github ningxu1995/OPERA) is a different system with different authors; it is not a collision.

scope.note: A multi-agent system (Lead Investigator, Method Builder, Experimentalist, Critical Reviewer, plus support sub-agents) running long-horizon studies: literature, hypothesis, code, physical measurement, analysis and manuscript writing. It is not a base model, a deep-research writer or a component.

autonomy.note: A5 is supported by the main text, which describes observed physical closure. The agent writes experimental code and invokes 'calibrated routines on the physical optical platform' (laser, SLM, power meter, two CMOS cameras). It acquires measurements (a 256x256 transmission matrix from 1,025 calibrated measurements) and revises its next action from the results. In a 206-step open-ended study it proposed and then physically validated an optical bilinear interaction (4-token XOR and 8-token experiments). Caveats for the notes: (a) the arXiv v1 PDF I extracted (25 pages) refers to 'Methods' and 'Supplementary Note' sections that it does not contain, so setup details and any human involvement (platform build and alignment, provision of calibration routines, diffuser changes) could not be checked; (b) the main text describes no human gates. All claims are self-reported in preprints that have not been peer reviewed. The kissing-number study is in-silico (A4) and does not affect the A5 rating.

access.note: Correction: paper-only -> open-data. The engine and hardware-control code are confirmed unreleased: Zenodo says 'The Qiushi Engine core system and hardware-control software are not included'. However, licensed research outputs are public: (1) Zenodo 19890402 (source data, analysis scripts, figures) under licence cc-by-4.0 (metadata.license); (2) Oxelra-AI/Qiushi-Engine-Kissing-Number-Research has a LICENSE file (MIT for original software and verification tools, CC BY 4.0 for reports and data; GitHub spdx NOASSERTION because the licence file is split). The optical GitHub repo has no licence (API license null; the README says 'No repository-wide license is asserted'). Catalogue precedent for an unreleased agent with public, licensed outputs is open-data: AlphaEvolve (results-only repo), AI Cosmologist (config and outputs only), Rainbow (A5, Zenodo data). Under that precedent, paper-only understates what is public. oxelra.com describes no sign-up or user access, so platform does not apply. If the maintainer prefers paper-only, the record is still admissible, since a ZJU physical-lab demonstration meets the significance bar.

category.note: physics fits: free-space optics experiments, plus discrete-geometry maths, which falls under physics by catalogue precedent. The optical experiments dominate.

urls.note: All proposed paper and repo URLs returned 200. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19890402 redirects to zenodo.org/records/19890402 (200). Both GitHub HTML URLs return 200. The repo labels need small fixes: the kissing-number label should state its licence (MIT code / CC BY 4.0 content). The optical GitHub label ('no licence') is accurate.

text.note: Mostly factual; the numbers (206 steps, 1,288.1 min, 145.9M tokens, 3,242 LLM calls, 1,242 tool calls, 163 notes, 44 scripts) match the abstract and README. Corrections: (1) 'operated commercially as Oxelra by Hangzhou Aosila Technology' overstates the source. The site says Oxelra is 'an AI company' using Qiushi Engine as its core (about page), and the operator appears only in Chinese as 杭州奥思拉科技有限公司; the English name 'Hangzhou Aosila Technology' is a transliteration not shown on the site (UNVERIFIED). No commercial offering is documented. (2) Drop 'Oxelra' as an alias: it names the company and platform brand, not the engine. Use the verified Chinese name 求是引擎 instead. (3) Add to the notes that the arXiv v1 PDF lacks the Methods and Supplementary Notes it cites.

scope.note: In scope by precedent. The paper reports agent-driven multi-step DFT workflows: 135 autonomous solid-state calculations, 98 molecular optimizations, and a six-step anomalous Hall conductivity pipeline with cross-session knowledge accumulation and reflection. Compare the MCP agent platforms already catalogued: ChemMCP, ParaView-MCP, MCP-SIM, VASPilot. Adversarial point: QMatSuite is mainly an MCP platform driven by an external general agent (Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI), which puts it close to the 'scientific software component' exclusion. It stays in scope because the contribution is the agent knowledge loop itself (record_insight, review_insight, search_knowledge, list_insights) and the paper evaluates it as an agent system.

autonomy.note: A3 is supported and conservative. Observed closure: an external LLM agent plans, executes and interprets multi-step simulations through MCP, and reflection sessions revise its knowledge base. All closure is computational (QE, Wannier90, ORCA), so A5 is ruled out. A3-A4 would also be defensible, because reflection sessions synthesize cross-compound patterns used for a quantitative prediction for InP. Tasks are human-specified, though, so A3 stands. The paper states that human review is expected before publication.

decisions.name: FUSION: a skill-based research agent for publicly obtainable nuclear-physics codes
decisions.rationale: The October hold was a scope question (should a domain skill pack shipped for general coding agents be admitted?), with an explicit trigger: 'if VALG, a Codex-only skill bundle, is promoted, FUSION should be promoted for consistency'. The baseline now shows VALG displayed as physics/open-source (date_added 2026-10-10; record says it runs inside Codex without a standalone runtime), and SolutionsX (an agent toolkit for external coding agents) was added the same day, so the scope condition is resolved. What changed at FUSION itself: arXiv v2 (2026-10-24) and the repository (commit of 2026-10-24) retire the bundled opencode fork; FUSION is now a plugin of 28 skills plus an offline literature collection, packaged for Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity, Gemini CLI and opencode. This removes the 'own runtime' argument used in October, but under the VALG precedent a runtime is not required. Licence: the LICENSE file is the MIT text plus an appended scope notice (MIT covers the repository; the driven physics codes are fetched from upstream under their own terms, some non-open, e.g. Sky3D under the CPC non-profit licence). GitHub's detector therefore reports NOASSERTION, but the text is MIT, and the abstract and arXiv comment both state MIT; the plugin itself carries no commercial-use restriction, so access is open-source with the third-party-code caveat in notes. Demonstrated closure is computational (A3): a recorded one-sentence request led to a FRESCO run with verified deck, convergence study and second-solver check, EXFOR retrieval, reporting the absence of 50 MeV data and comparing at the measured energies. Limits: single author, beta, 'not used by anyone else' per README; physical judgment stays with the user. Note the only GitHub release is v0.1.0 (2026-08-11, fork era); the README calls the current state v0.2.0 but there is no v0.2.0 tag or release. No same-name collision in the baseline.

decisions.rationale: Material change. arXiv v2 (2026-10-23) renames the system from MAESTRO to DREAMS (data retrieval, extraction, and multi-scale screening) and adds Data and Code availability sections. Data: the agent-curated DREAMS COD database (36,130 computation-ready CIFs from 27,922 COD structures, with metadata and computed properties) is published on Zenodo under CC BY 4.0 by authors Chen Yuntong and Zhao Guobin; this meets the October alternative condition 'the curated computation-ready MOF database ... under a stated licence', although no decision traces are in the deposit. Code: the paper says all source code is on GitHub at ClearPathLab/DREAMS (MIT LICENSE, CPLab, organisation created 2026-10-03), but today the repository holds only an 'Initial commit' with LICENSE, README and .gitignore (pushed 2026-10-21), and the cited code archive DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23589225 returns 404. So the record enters as open-data, following the AI Cosmologist and AI CUDA Engineer precedent (released outputs, agent code not yet public), and upgrades to open-source when the code lands. v2 also changes the autonomy evidence: v1 said no manual intervention in the continuous-update run, while v2 states each task plan was confirmed by a researcher before execution, and screening results receive human validation; hence A3-A4, not A4. NAME COLLISION: the catalog already has asa-dreams (DREAMS, Viswanathan group DFT agent, arXiv 2507.14267, BattModels/material_agent), a different system; the new record needs a disambiguated name and id. Significant beyond padding: end-to-end literature-to-simulation pipeline over 400,000 papers and 64,071 CSD-derived curated structures, plus a released database.

On promotion use a distinct id/name (e.g. asa-dreams-mof, 'DREAMS (MOF discovery agent)'), alias MAESTRO (v1 abstract), autonomy A3 (A3-A4 at most) with the per-plan researcher approval and human result validation disclosed, category chemistry, and keep the Zenodo COD dataset (CC BY 4.0) as a data link.

decisions.name: BioLitBench / SCRIBE (What Can a Leaderboard Certify?)
decisions.rationale: The unresolved condition was data distribution, and it is now met. On 2026-10-14 the authors published the Hugging Face dataset shawnzhg/BioLitBench (revision v1.0, CC BY 4.0, public, not gated). The repository README now documents how to download it and rebuild the article text from PMC and PubMed with digest checks; frozen scoring files moved into the repository the same day. The second condition, whether BioLitBench stands alone as a record, I judge yes. It is a released benchmark with a public leaderboard of literature-review agents (SurveyG, AutoSurvey, LiRA, Claude Code, Elicit Systematic Review and others), scored claim by claim against published biomedical reviews, which fits the 'literature ... reporting' scope of multi-step scientific work. ResearchArena (survey/organisation benchmark) is precedent. The record is the benchmark. SCRIBE, the paper's trained agent (deployed at glkb.org per the dataset card), goes in the notes and not as a separate record, because it is a literature-review writing system close to the excluded general report-writing class. Limits: arXiv v1 only (2026-09-26, no withdrawal, not peer reviewed). The main contribution is a statistical certification method. The v1.0 data supports only the fixed-input track because no retrieval pool is released. The paper says 2,042 articles, while the dataset card tabulates 1,842 train plus 50 test tasks (plus test peers and exclusions).

decisions.name: SRHarness
decisions.rationale: The October hold was a lane and scope question: SRHarness is not an evaluation harness, so it was wrong for the benchmark lane. Re-read against the physics-lane precedents, it qualifies as an agent system. The paper (arXiv 2609.35501, now v2 of 2026-10-24, no withdrawal) and the README describe an LLM agent that analyses data, calls fitting, evaluation and code-execution tools, keeps evaluated hypotheses, and runs, branches and restarts long symbolic-regression searches up to formula submission. That is the same kind of system as the catalog's LLM-SR (physics, A2-A3) and SR-Scientist (physics, A3), and the paper compares itself directly against SR-Scientist. Release status has also matured: MIT licence text, PyPI sr-harness at v1.0.8, tagged releases v1.0.2 to v1.0.8 in the upstream repository, and the paper's Code availability names the tsinghua-fib-lab repository. Ownership note: tsinghua-fib-lab/SRHarness is a GitHub fork of yuzhTHU/SRHarness, the upstream the organisation README links to (same pattern as MechBench, forked from yuzhTHU/mdbench). Closure is in silico on LLM-SRBench data, so A3, not A4 or A5.

It is not in the baseline.

decisions.name: BioDesignBench (Romero Lab, Duke)
decisions.rationale: The paper exists and was missed in October because the repository README still says 'coming soon'. Europe PMC (PPR1211013) and the bioRxiv API show 'Benchmarking and behavioral characterization of LLM agents for protein design' by J. Kim and P. A. Romero (Duke). It is v1 of 2026-05-08 and v2 of 2026-06-28 (DOI 10.64898/2026.05.06.723381, preprint licence CC BY-NC), and its abstract introduces BioDesignBench with 76 expert-curated tasks. The second October condition, the 76-task set in the public release, will not be met by design. The paper's Data availability states that task specifications and ground truth are withheld to prevent contamination. Outside agents are evaluated through the public Hugging Face leaderboard, which accepts submissions, and per-task data is available under a data use agreement. This is a deliberate hidden-test benchmark from an established lab, with an open harness, reference agents, a 17-tool MCP server and a submission leaderboard. That meets the bar, with access recorded as platform (hosted scoring) rather than open-source or open-data. Licence discrepancy: the paper says MIT for the evaluation framework, but the repository LICENSE and GitHub detection are Apache-2.0. Both are open licences; record the file. No name collision found; distinct from the catalog's PRAXIS (Romero Lab A5 protein-engineering system).

The README's License section says 'Code: MIT', the paper's Code availability says MIT, and the HF Space card says license: mit. The 76 tasks, inputs and ground truth are withheld (paper Data availability; README) and can be used only by submitting to the hosted leaderboard (HF Space runtime stage RUNNING, public, not gated) or through a data use agreement. scope.note: Multi-step in-silico experimental workflow: natural-language question, then structured request, Review, Route (data/model/adapter selection), Run (deterministic Virtual Experiment DAG), then Results with report, trace and provenance, or structured abstention. This matches catalogued perturbation agents (BioDiscoveryAgent, CellForge, PerTurboAgent). Arguable counterpoint: the paper calls itself a 'programmable Virtual Cell runtime', and the agent is a thin orchestration layer whose LLM cannot produce numbers. That layer still plans and executes multi-step virtual experiments end to end, so I do not judge it a mere software component.

autonomy.note: A3 is supported: a fixed five-stage workflow running registered predictors, with no hypothesis-iteration loop (so not A4) and no wet-lab loop (not A5). The CLI example passes a '--yes' flag, which hints at a confirmation step; its exact semantics were not checked.

decisions.rationale: Scope decision taken today. The preprint (York University / Vector Institute; only v1, 2026-09-16) and the MIT repository describe a model system: Cell2Sentence/Gemma experts trained by contrastive LoRA adaptation and task adapters, with an orchestrator that routes free-form questions about a ranked expression profile to expert small language models under an optimised playbook. scope.note: The system is a domain-specific agentic research environment, not a general deep-research writer. In the paper, the Agentic Research Director runs a multi-round graph-of-thoughts search with knowledge-graph sampling, GNN link prediction and retrieval tools, scoring and pruning, a validation layer and persistent memory across rounds. The output is ranked hypotheses that were then tested experimentally. This is in scope by the precedent of the hosted commercial platforms PromptBio, Kosmos and Microsoft Discovery.

autonomy.note: A3 is supported and conservative. Closure is in silico only: the system generated and ranked hypotheses. Humans chose the four tested combinations by 'internal vetting of the 20 top-ranked' candidates (Table 3 caption). The in vitro work was contracted to Pharmaron, under protocols the authors designed and with data the authors interpreted. Lab-in-the-loop and self-driving-lab connectivity appear only in marketing and were not demonstrated, so A5 does not apply. The human selection gate should be disclosed in the notes (see correction).

access.note: 'platform' is correct. emet.benchsci.com is live and login-gated: it redirects 307 to /auth/login, then to id.summit.benchsci.com/authorize. The home page offers 'Try EMET for free' and 'Academic sign up'. The pricing page lists a Free Academic tier ('Limited access to the BenchSci platform') and Custom Enterprise ('Start with a free pilot'). The preprint has no code or data availability statement, and no public repository was found, so the product is proprietary and there is no licence to record. access_evidence could cite the pricing page. The Hypothesis Generation Agent itself was announced on 10 Sept as coming 'to Emet customers in the next couple of weeks'; whether free or academic users can reach it is UNVERIFIED.

category.note: 'biology' fits: preclinical drug discovery, disease biology and target identification. Precedent: PromptBio is also 'biology'.

urls.note: All proposed URLs resolve: the bioRxiv v2 abs and full text, /platform, the launch news post and /pricing all return 200. https://benchsci.com returns 307 to https://www.benchsci.com/, which returns 200; the proposal logged 200, which is the status after the redirect. https://emet.benchsci.com/ returns 307 to /auth/login and then to the BenchSci IdP. The proposal said 302 straight to the IdP; it is login-gated either way. I recommend adding the first-party Hypothesis Generation Agent post as a source.

text.note: The notes say 'The four top-ranked combinations were tested'. The paper says the four were selected 'following internal vetting of the 20 top-ranked' candidates. The abstract's 'four highest-ranked' simplifies this, and the human selection gate needs to be disclosed. Other claims match the sources: 1.5 billion triples and 100+ databases; CRO Pharmaron; CDC7+PKMYT1 synergy in two lines; two of four combinations active. Marketing figures differ: the product pages say 2.2B edges and 858M nodes, the paper says 1.5B triples. The record correctly uses the paper's figure. I also suggest naming the productized capability (Hypothesis Generation Agent) and the limited academic tier.

decisions.name: PEN-STACK
decisions.rationale: Both October conditions are now resolved. (1) Licensed release: the repository ahmedanees-m/pen-stack is MIT-licensed and owned by the first author; its README carries an arXiv 2608.20412 badge and CITATION.cff cites the arXiv ID. It is also on PyPI (pen-stack 0.2.0, MIT) and Zenodo (concept DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21787136; record v0.1.0, MIT, same three authors). So the release is first-party and author-endorsed. (2) Scope: the paper calls itself a tool layer, but the repository ships its own agent layer. That layer includes a co-scientist that turns a goal into distinct, verified, cited strategies, a write planner, and a gated design-build-test-learn loop, which the docs place at self-driving-lab Level 3, in silico, with a human at every gate. Catalog precedent is ToolUniverse, an agent-tool infrastructure row at A2. I assign A2-A3. The closed loop runs only against a simulated lab, so it is not A5. The arXiv abs page shows v1 only, with no withdrawal notice. HTML full text is still 404, so the claims rest on the abstract and the repository docs. Companion adjudication: BioFirewall (arXiv 2608.20413, repository ahmedanees-m/bio-firewall, Apache-2.0) is rule-based biosecurity middleware that screens agent plans. It is a governance component, not a scientific agent, so it is folded into this record's notes and not added as a row. Curator caution: this is a young single-group academic project with 3 GitHub stars, and its headline grounding result rests on a small audit.
